title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
description: Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid
body:
Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6054139/nx-s1-10020784" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  Puerto Rico's supreme court has ruled the island's governor can kick out the private company that's been running its troubled power grid for five years. The decision could have huge consequences for electric service in Puerto Rico. Here is NPR's Adrian Florido.ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's already rickety power grid in 2017, the island's government privatized it. It gave a company called LUMA Energy, based in Canada and Texas, a 15-year deal to take over the power lines, promising that LUMA would rebuild the grid stronger and improve the notoriously unreliable service. LUMA took over in 2021. But things have not gone as planned.Blackouts are still a constant fact of life. LUMA has come in for harsh criticism from customers and officials. Last year, Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez-Colon filed suit to nullify LUMA's contract. Yesterday, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court ruled in her favor that LUMA must go.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JENNIFFER GONZALEZ-COLON: Today is a day of celebration on the island.FLORIDO: This is the governor speaking after the ruling. She said LUMA has not lived up to its promises.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GONZALEZ-COLON: More outages on the island, more shutdowns on the island. They have not fulfilled the requirements of the contract.FLORIDO: In fact, the island's supreme court ruled on procedural grounds, saying officials had not followed local requirements when approving agreements with the company. The court gave the local government a year to put a new operator in place. The governor said the work to find a new private company will start immediately.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GONZALEZ-COLON: It's going to be a good transition. We're going to make it in a year. And I hope that all companies that are interested in participating in this process will fulfill and follow the process of law. And we're going to be opening that process for public bid.FLORIDO: The court gave LUMA Energy 10 days to request a reconsideration of its ruling. In a statement, LUMA said it is considering its legal options. The company has long argued that the grid it took over was in awful shape and that it is not fully to blame for the blackouts. A new operator will need approval from both the local government and a federal oversight board that Congress put in place 10 years ago to get Puerto Rico out of bankruptcy. In a statement, that board criticized the governor for ending LUMA' s contract without having a new company ready to go. It said it's worried about the continuity of service on the island. In her remarks yesterday, the governor said she has a plan in place and will reveal it soon.Adrian Florido, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF TOBACCO'S "BACKWOODS ALTAR")

title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
description: U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schu
body:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY), center, is seen here meeting with newly elected Democratic Senators, (L-R) Senator-elect Andy Kim (D-NJ), Senator-elect Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Senator-elect Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) Senator-elect Adam Schiff (D-CA) Senator-elect Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Senator-elect Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 12, 2024. That group of senators is pushing to add an incoming freshman senator to the leadership ranks.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.    "The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."    The letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.    The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.    
   "These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."    Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.   "On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.    New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW  that leadership extends beyond the top post.    "This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."   The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.    Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.    
   "Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.    On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

title: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
description:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
    
            
                
                T
body:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6052417/nx-s1-10019261" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., speaks at a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing in Washington on Sept. 21, 2022.
                
                    Samuel Corum/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Samuel Corum/Getty Images
    

   
   Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.   U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.   There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.   
   Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.   Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.   For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.   "What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.   Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.   "The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.   Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.   "Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."   The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.   
   In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.   Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.   The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer.

title: The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
description: In an aerial view, a container ship arri
body:
In an aerial view, a container ship arrives at the Port of Oakland on Oct. 10, 2025 in Oakland, Calif.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.   That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.   The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.   
   NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.   The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.   The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."   However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.   
   According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.   According to the U.S. official, in some cases, employees aboard the ships suspected something nefarious was going on when they noticed email disruptions or couldn't log in to their accounts, or, in at least one case, an extended communications blackout. The U.S. official declined to comment on how the U.S. government knows about the extent of breaches across the sector.   
   However, according to the U.S. official, hackers were able to break in using the Fortinet vulnerability and then pivot from the ships' IT systems over to their network of devices controlling physical processes on the ships, what's called operational technology.   
   The U.S. official said the bad actors "could have impacted the systems on board that control propulsion, steering, navigation, and cargo management," though they did not share any examples of that kind of activity occurring. In at least one case, one of the ships affected was an LNG tanker designed to transport liquified natural gas. It's important to keep systems at a certain temperature to prevent dangerous accidents if a ship's cargo includes explosive materials –from chemicals to fuel.   While commercial vessels are accustomed to physical security reviews entering the United States following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, digital threats are becoming all the more important to track as adversaries can break in and cause damage from afar. "It's a totally new paradigm that these tankers are networked in this way," the U.S. official said.   Even so, national security officials have feared something like this might happen for years. A former Navy official who requested anonymity to discuss internal operations tells NPR that "we had been tracking the possibility to exploit and take control of [operational technology] systems on Navy ships and Merchant [Marine] ships for a long time, and now this is coming to fruition."   While the U.S. government is wary of advertising Iranian hacking efforts during the war, officials also want to spread awareness of the vulnerability of internet connected devices, particularly those that are linked to the technology that controls critical processes. "These are not sophisticated attacks," the official said. "This is a known vulnerability that could be mitigated with some pretty basic cyber hygiene."   
   "Modern ships are highly integrated systems. A cyberattack presents significant risks, including the potential for a collision, grounding, oil spill, or even an explosion. The Coast Guard regularly publishes bulletins on cyber vulnerabilities and actions vessel owners and operators can take to secure their networks," according to a statement from the Coast Guard.   Ahead of the winter and a busy holiday season for commercial shipping, officials are bracing themselves to investigate any ship entering U.S. ports that could be compromised.   "People never think about what a modern blessing electricity is until it goes out. People take the marine transportation system for granted until there's a problem and their stuff doesn't get there by Christmas," the U.S. official said. "I wish more Americans knew how complex this system is."

title: Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., shares why he opposes Trump's proposed tariffs
description: NPR's A Martinez speaks with Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine about the Democrat's opposition to President Trump's new tariffs.
body:
NPR's A Martinez speaks with Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine about the Democrat's opposition to President Trump's new tariffs.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  All right. Let's go now to one of the lawmakers who's been trying to fight the president's tariffs in Congress. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia backed multiple bills meant to curb or refund the administration's tariffs, including legislation that would constrain the president's ability to impose new tariffs at all.Senator, happy Thanksgiving. Thanks for joining us on Turkey Day.TIM KAINE: A, very glad to be with you. And our Turkey Day is going to cost about 6% more than it cost last year...MARTÍNEZ: (Laughter).KAINE: ...Partly because of tariffs. So this is a good topic.MARTÍNEZ: Well, let's get into that. So the president says the objective is to counter unfair foreign trade practices. What's your view of that rationale?KAINE: Well, in the big picture, what the president has said is this tariff strategy applied everywhere is going to increase manufacturing jobs in the United States. To the contrary, manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined during President Trump's second term. He also said it would reduce our trade deficit. The trade deficit has increased during President Trump's second term. So neither of the goals that he has have been achieved by his tariff strategy. And one of the things he promised to do - bring prices down - has been dramatically affected in the negative way you saw the inflation numbers yesterday. We're seeing dramatic inflation driven by tariffs in the Iran war. So this is an economic strategy that is a big failure.MARTÍNEZ: You mentioned manufacturing jobs are not happening in the way that we were told they would happen. But how do you square that with the Steelworkers Union who says that the new tariffs are long overdue?KAINE: There are particular sectors that like them. I mean, the steel industry likes more steel production in the U.S. But overall, if you look at manufacturing, generally, manufacturing jobs are down. They were up during the Biden administration. They're down during the Trump administration with President Trump saying that the tariffs were going to cause this big manufacturing renaissance.MARTÍNEZ: So I mentioned your efforts in the Senate to fight the president's tariffs. What is your strongest argument for passing legislation to stop the president from imposing these particular tariffs?KAINE: So there's a broad argument, and then there's kind of a narrow focused one. So here's the broad one. The Constitution gives tariff power to Congress, not the president. And Congresses of both parties, in my view, have made mistakes over decades in handing off this power, delegating it to the president and allowing the president to impose tariffs on his own. Just to allow one person to impose taxes is not a good idea. And so there are a variety of strategies. I - we - I did work with Senator Paul of Kentucky, and we led the effort against the president's use of the IEEPA statute to impose tariffs. The Supreme Court ultimately struck down...MARTÍNEZ: International Emergency Economic Powers Act, yeah.KAINE: That's right, yeah. And the Supreme Court ultimately struck down any imposition of tariffs under that statute. But we're looking at the remaining statutes that Congress has sort of handed the power to the president in one of two ways. You can either repeal those statutes and eliminate any presidential ability to impose tariffs. Or recognizing that presidents sometimes need to move quick - quicker than Congress can - you could allow the president to impose tariffs for a limited period of time, say 60 or 90 days, but those tariffs would expire unless Congress affirmatively validates them and continues them.So those are some of the legal solutions that are on the table. And with Democratic majorities, I think we have a very good chance of getting some of these bills to President Trump's desk.MARTÍNEZ: You have 56 U.S. senators in - next year. What's the likelihood that you're going to get enough Republicans that share your view? You mentioned Rand Paul, but you're going to need more if you want to pass legislation that the president can't veto.KAINE: We will. We - my prediction is we're going to get enough Republican votes in the aftermath of the election, which was really a repudiation of tariffs and the war. We'll get enough Republican votes to put tariff bills on President Trump's desk. Now, here comes the next challenge. If he vetoes those bills, would we have enough to have a two-thirds vote in both Houses to override his veto? That's a - more of an uphill climb. But we're going to test that. We're going to put bills on his desk, dramatically limiting his tariff powers to try to help Americans' pocketbooks. And then we'll say to him, if you veto this bill, you're just going to hurt people. So why don't you just sign it?MARTÍNEZ: What message do you think these new tariffs are sending to U.S. trading partners? I mean, it's been a few years of, you know, going back and forth on tariffs.KAINE: Yeah. A, I mentioned there's sort of a narrower argument on tariffs, and now you're asking me about that. Tariffs have a place. And I think most have agreed that China has been really ripping off the United States in trade. You know, theft of intellectual property, state subsidies of industries that then try to undercut American jobs. The strategy up to President Trump had always been, let's link arms with our allies - the EU, Japan, Korea, Canada. And let's all impose consequences on China for being a trade rule violator. The message that's being sent by the Trump administration is, hey, we're decoupling with allies, and we're just going to wage war individually against all of you. That makes the effort against China much less likely to succeed than if we instead linked our arms with our allies, didn't impose tariffs against them, and focused at what I think everybody agrees is the main trade violator in the world, which is China.MARTÍNEZ: Senator, we've got about 30 seconds left. Have you thought about what the next two years are going to be like to try and work together with the president to make Americans' lives more - less expensive?KAINE: I think what the Dems need to do is put a lot of bills on his desk. And we can get Republican help on some, but we also have some mechanisms like budget reconciliation where we can do bills just with Democratic votes. Put good bills on his desk that help everyday people and say, Mr. President, if you want to help folks, you'll sign this. And if you don't sign it, you're going to let people know you don't care about them.MARTÍNEZ: All right. That is Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia. Once again, happy Thanksgiving and thanks for coming on.KAINE: Thanks, A. Be good.

title: Trump administration proposes new tariffs on goods from major U.S. trading partners
description:
President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates.   

    
        
          T
body:
President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on goods from 14 of the U.S.'s biggest trading partners, including Japan, the EU and China. It's arguing that these new tariffs fight other countries' unfair trade practices, but it's not clear that they will actually do that.For more, we have NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, what did the White House outline yesterday?DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Well, it's new proposed tariffs on goods from major trading partners - the ones you mentioned, and also South Korea and Cambodia, for example. And the rates could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, also 35% on goods from Vietnam and 20 or 25% on goods from other countries. They're also proposing additional tariffs on sugar and aircrafts from Brazil, and that would add to previous tariffs the U.S. imposed there.MARTÍNEZ: When could these plans actually become real?KURTZLEBEN: Well, they could go into effect within a couple of months. That's what U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said yesterday. Now, as for what the rates will be, well, that's still unclear, and that's because for each country, excepting those additional tariffs on Brazil, the White House has two rates they've listed - a proposed rate and a deal rate. To give an example, the tariff on China could be 20%. That's the deal rate. But depending in part on how ongoing discussions go, the rates on Chinese goods could go as high as 40%.MARTÍNEZ: Forty percent. Now, yeah, the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's earlier tariffs. So how is the White House legally justifying these new ones?KURTZLEBEN: Well, these are being implemented under a law known for short as Section 301, which is meant to counter other countries' unfair trade practices. And so here the White House is alleging that these other countries have what's called structural excess capacity in various manufactured goods. And the administration has described this as when another country has policies that cause a good to be overproduced, which then distorts a global market for that good. And so those practices, according to the administration, can include all sorts of things, like labor practices, subsidies and tax breaks.Now, the administration imposed other sweeping 301 tariffs earlier this year, and there's a lawsuit in process challenging those, with the key argument being that those tariffs were just way broader than the 301 law calls for.MARTÍNEZ: Now, you mentioned a lawsuit. Could these new tariffs face similar legal challenges?KURTZLEBEN: You know, they could. We'll see what happens. But I talked to Sara Albrecht. She's chairman and CEO of the nonpartisan Liberty and Justice Center (ph), which filed that lawsuit against those earlier tariffs. And she said these new tariffs are not being used the way 301 tariffs are supposed to.SARA ALBRECHT: It is a negotiating tactic. That is not what tariffs, in a broad sense, are supposed to be. Like, you can do that on a country-by-country basis if they're addressing a specific problem, not just general, hey, we want better trade deals.KURTZLEBEN: In addition, both she and other trade experts say they think the White House is just proposing these new tariffs as a way to replace the sweeping tariffs the Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.MARTÍNEZ: Now, we all just found out how unpopular these tariffs were in the midterm elections. So how are these new tariffs landing politically?KURTZLEBEN: Well, we've heard some real pushback from congressional Democrats. Richard Neal, top House Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement, quote, "Trump is putting everything from family budgets to our national security at risk to keep his tariff scheme in place."Now, congressional Republicans have been quieter, and this does come a few weeks after they lost dozens of seats in the election, which is widely attributed, in large part, to high prices, and tariffs do cause higher prices.MARTÍNEZ: All right, that's NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, thanks a lot.KURTZLEBEN: Of course.

title: U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump
description: Under Chairman Brendan Carr, left, the F
body:
Under Chairman Brendan Carr, left, the Federal Communications Commission launched an early review of Disney's licenses to operate all the local ABC stations it owns. New Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro, right, says the company is fighting back to protect ABC's journalistic integrity and free speech. "We're very principled on this," he said.
                
                    Heather Diehl/Thibault Camus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Diehl/Thibault Camus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge has blocked President Trump and his administration from taking action to challenge the ABC television network's broadcast licenses, finding it to be an unconstitutional punishment for satire, commentary and news coverage that Trump doesn't like.   
   In her preliminary injunction filed Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan found that the federal agency's early reviews represented retaliation for speech the Trump administration resented.   Such perceived offenses included late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's jabs at the president, the critical remarks of hosts on the chat show The View, and the moderation of a presidential debate in September 2024.   ABC and its corporate parent, the Walt Disney Co., serve six of the 10 largest markets in the U.S., including New York, Los Angeles, and Houston. They contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.   
   "Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face -- loss of their broadcast licenses -- the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," Judge AliKhan wrote.   She rejected the Trump administration's motion to dismiss the lawsuit from ABC and Disney challenging the review of the local licenses. Usually the licenses last eight years and are up for review on a staggered basis. They are rarely taken away.   In her ruling, AliKhan relied heavily on public statements and social media postings in which Trump attacked ABC and Disney, as well as posts by Trump's pick as the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr.   "What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC 'can keep getting a license' if it 'report[s] fake news,' ... has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions," she wrote. "The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years -- the most recent being in July 2026."   And the judge cited the administration's "tangible steps toward enforcing President Trump and Commissioner Carr's repeated threats to strip the Plaintiff Stations of their licenses."   
   "Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," Judge AliKhan wrote.   Carr did not respond to NPR's request for comment Wednesday evening.   ABC hailed the ruling in a statement as "an important victory for the First Amendment."   Among the targets of ire from Trump and Carr was ABC's decision not to broadcast Trump's July 2026 Oval Office address on its television network. ABC's legal team said the network streamed it on its digital news service, but would not have done so absent the political pressure from the FCC.   It is one of several examples of newsroom decisions made under duress, the network's lawyers said in court. Kimmel's interview with then-Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico of Texas was uploaded to YouTube instead of being aired on ABC's late night television show. (Talarico won election to the U.S. Senate earlier this month.) And The View stopped hosting candidates for political office in 2026 in the months ahead of the fall elections.   
   Judge AliKhan rejected arguments from the FCC that the court could not take action because it has not yet rejected the license renewals. The very act of premature review for retaliatory reasons is unconstitutional and unlawful – and hard to reverse, she wrote.   "For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct," said Anna M. Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC. "Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I've said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side."   This ruling comes six weeks after a parallel ruling in a case brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico against the Trump administration for restricting access. Officials barred journalists from the three news outlets from the White House after Trump lambasted them for "purposefully negative" news coverage.   
   In that case, U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, writing, "It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him." That, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation. The administration is appealing. And despite the ruling, the White House continues to limit the three news outlets' access to the president.   Disney's shift in strategy   In December 2024, just a few weeks before Trump became president for the second time, Disney agreed to settle a lawsuit Trump had brought against ABC News by paying $16 million, including legal fees. Many outside legal experts believed Disney would have had the upper hand if it had stuck it out in court.   Now under new leadership, Disney has drawn the line at what it contends is a threat to its broadcast licenses — and profits — over its editorial independence.   "We're very principled on this," Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told CNBC in August, just days before the company filed its lawsuit. "We're going to stand up to what we believe is journalistic integrity, and we're not going to be told how to run that side of our business." D'Amaro became chief executive in March.   The FCC had already kicked off an investigation of Disney's diversity practices when it announced the review.   
   Carr, the agency's chief, has said it initiated the review of Disney's broadcast licenses over concerns that the company engaged in racial discrimination through its diversity, equity and inclusion actions.   "Obviously, the Disney lawsuit is without merit," Carr told NPR in August. "From our perspective, we're going to continue to follow the facts and the law wherever they may lead."   Judge AliKhan wrote in her order that Disney had been responsive to every query that the FCC had made in the diversity investigation. Carr said in a statement to a congresswoman that he found the responses to be "deficient, nonresponsive, and disingenuous."   
   The FCC generally reviews broadcast licenses once every eight years. The decision to examine Disney's licenses now is remarkable in two ways: Reviews of a company's licenses are usually staggered, rather than all at once. Additionally, some of Disney's licenses are not due for renewal for another several years. It is considered an essentially unprecedented act for the FCC to take.   Justice Department lawyers conceded the FCC had other ways to investigate DEI   In a court hearing in October, Disney's legal team argued it was suffering irreparable harm to its First Amendment freedoms as a result of the swift move to review the licenses.   Lead Disney attorney Beth Wilkinson compared the reviews to a "guillotine blade" hanging above the company, ready to fall at any moment. (Judge AliKhan thanked her for not comparing it to the Sword of Damocles of Greek legend.)   U.S. Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel shrugged off that claim. But his arguments led to a series of telling and dramatic exchanges with the judge.   Georgiev-Remmel contended that the review was a useful "tool" the FCC was deploying to secure more complete information for the diversity investigation. He said the agency was having trouble eliciting necessary information from Disney.   Disney's Wilkinson seized on the claim, asserting it proved that the license review was unnecessary. And she noted that the FCC only informed Disney that it was dissatisfied with the information the company had provided about its diversity practices 17 days after the reviews had been announced. That gave the company little time to stave off the nearly unprecedented process by fulfilling the requests.   Judge AliKhan asked Georgiev-Remmel what other tools the agency had at its disposal to get that information.   The Justice Department trial lawyers representing the FCC appeared to be caught off guard. Georgiev-Remmel initially said he wasn't sure.   
   Some minutes later, after conferring with colleagues, Georgiev-Remmel said the FCC could have subpoenaed the information, fined Disney, or taken other measures. But he said the agency could decide to set the reviews aside should Disney provide sufficient information.   The judge appeared immediately skeptical that the instant license reviews were a necessary or even reasonable step to achieve that.   A second judicial rebuke   In both Disney's lawsuit against the FCC and CNN, MS NOW and Politico's suit against the White House, the media companies argued that the Trump administration had violated their constitutional rights of free speech and due process. The Justice Department argued other priorities and prerogatives were in play: national security in one, the need to pursue an investigation into diversity practices in the other.   
   And in both, the judges expressed incredulity or skepticism that the Trump administration had acted in good faith.   As in matters beyond the realm of media, the Trump administration is pressing to expand its authority and powers. The White House access case would effectively require a reversal of decades of precedent on closely related cases.   In the case of ABC, the Trump administration wants the ability to trip up broadcasters who put things on the air that offend the president – simply because that technology falls under government regulation.   Even during all this litigation, the Justice Department initiated an anti-trust investigation into the five networks – including ABC and CNN – that make up the White House video pool sharing footage and duties to other outlets. The networks have been collaborating since their inception.   What caught the attention of the administration? The fact that the networks consulted before deciding not to substitute another channel in for CNN -- on the increasing number of days the president's aides blocked it from serving as the pool representative covering Trump's public appearances in small spaces that cannot accommodate the large contingent of reporters that cover the White House.      
   Stay up to date on politics news and analysis that matter with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly

title: Moving to Florida may become a choice of some Republicans after midterms
description: In Florida, Republicans kept power of state government after the midterms. It's now the largest state where the GOP is still in charge.
body:
In Florida, Republicans kept power of state government after the midterms. It's now the largest state where the GOP is still in charge.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Florida is the largest state in the country where Republicans kept control after the midterms. Some credit conservatives who moved there in recent years, like Republican Michael Fusella.MICHAEL FUSELLA: So I think that they actually have a lot to thank us for, and they should be grateful that we're here.DETROW: Meghan Bowman with member station WUSF in Tampa reports that the trend could continue post-midterms.MEGHAN BOWMAN, BYLINE: Democratic candidates made gains in Florida in the midterms and won a few more seats in the state legislature, but Republicans still control all branches of Florida's government.FUSELLA: It's been that, like, shining beacon on the hill for the country.BOWMAN: Republican voter Michael Fusella says he's proud his party held strong here.FUSELLA: This was a blue tsunami, but I also think it was a red wildfire. Wildfires, they burn everything down in sight. However, wildfires are actually good. They rejuvenate the soil, and that - it grows back even stronger, right?BOWMAN: Fusella moved to Tampa from New Jersey about four years ago. He says Florida Republicans held the line election night because of people like him.FUSELLA: So many conservatives, like myself, fled these Democrat states, especially from up north, and came down here and helped change Florida into the conservative stronghold that it is today.BOWMAN: That was especially true during the COVID years. And now there are signs some Texans might consider the Sunshine State.(CHEERING)BOWMAN: People in Austin cheered when Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico won in the notoriously red state. But for conservative voters like Reigen Lox in suburban Dallas, the news wasn't as exciting.REIGEN LOX: I had an inkling that something could change, but I didn't expect it on this large of a scale. And I think that is concerning for a lot of people in Texas.BOWMAN: Now Lox is considering moving to Florida based on the midterm results. Marie Bailey is a conservative and a realtor in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. She started a Facebook group for people leaving California and moving to Texas. Now she's considering moving herself.MARIE BAILEY: Everyone was shocked at the election, and there's a lot of people that are rethinking their move. And we all know that Florida's a destination for people moving, but I think even more so now that Texas turned blue.BOWMAN: She says the beaches, amusement parks and cruise ports are a big draw. And with the midterm results, conservatives may be eyeing the state for its values. But Kirsten England, a political science professor at the University of South Florida, says it's unlikely a large influx of people are relocating solely because of the midterm results.KIRSTEN ENGLAND: If they were saying, oh, I'm going to move to Florida, well, then they already were thinking of it, and that's not the same thing.BOWMAN: Instead, what mostly brings people to Florida is age, says Sean Freeder. He's a political science professor at the University of North Florida.SEAN FREEDER: Florida has a unique role in the country where it acts as kind of an absorption sink for retirees and older folks.BOWMAN: And that, he says, refreshes Florida's conservative population in ways it doesn't in other states.FREEDER: Older retirees - we find in our data, it's not lefties moving from California and New York to Florida. It's Republicans.BOWMAN: And a recently passed amendment that will drastically lower property taxes could be another draw for people to move to Florida, says Tim Lyons. He's a Sarasota mortgage broker and co-manages a Facebook group to help people relocate. It has more than 32,000 members. He dismisses the idea that the midterms alone will bring more people to Florida.TIM LYONS: It's not about blue or red, necessarily. It just seems to be the same old things - weather, just the timing of their life.BOWMAN: Florida, he says, is a destination, no matter the politics. For NPR News, I'm Meghan Bowman in Tampa.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
description:
Storm Postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade, Trump's New Tariffs, Iowa Post-Detonation
    
            
                
                Tr
body:
Storm Postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade, Trump's New Tariffs, Iowa Post-Detonation
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-155950/nx-s1-mx-6054761-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons.
                
                    Adam Gray/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Adam Gray/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.   
   The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.   🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. For each country, the White House has listed a "proposed" rate and a "deal" rate, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. For example, if talks with China progress positively, they may receive a deal rate of 20%, which is different from its proposed rate of 40%. Although the Supreme Court overturned President Trump's previous tariffs, the new ones fall under Section 301, a law meant to counter unfair trade practices. The administration says these countries exhibit "structural excess capacity" in various manufactured goods, a situation caused by policies that lead to overproduction, which can distort the global market.   Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.   
   🎧 Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio says the major concern is the potential release of lead into the air from the explosion. She adds that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has tested the area since the detonation and hasn't found lead in the air. The EPA has deployed around 300 people to sample the air, ground and nearby water. Lead is a neurotoxin that especially endangers children and pregnant people because it can impede childhood development. After a week and a half of delays and inconsistent communication from the Army, residents have grown hesitant about the Army and the EPA's initial findings, Billingham says. Residents want independent monitoring and the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are conducting regional sampling. Results are expected in a few days and should show if their measurements align with the EPA's data, Billingham says.   A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
                
                    J Studios/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        J Studios/Getty Images
    

   
   Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.   
   🛒 Delete the app or remove your credit card info if you have one-click checkout with a company.🛒 Add an item to your online shopping cart and leave it for 24 hours. Research shows that delaying a purchase decreases your interest in it.🛒 Make intentional choices. Don't reject all new things. After you understand this, you can learn to say no to the wrong items and yes to the right ones.🛒 Revisiting old things can provide you with untapped enjoyment in them, research has found. You can apply this by rereading a book or by traveling to a city you have visited before.   For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Andrea Starr
    

   
   Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers walks off the field after their 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on Nov. 22, 2026, in Philadelphia.
                
                    Emilee Chinn/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Emilee Chinn/Getty Images
    

   
   The Pittsburgh Steelers have cut quarterback Aaron Rodgers after he claimed in an interview that the team's head coach sleeps in meetings.The Ariston Cafe opened in 1924 along Illinois's Route 66, serving classic American diner fare. The National Register landmark attracts international travelers and hosts local milestones, from wedding proposals to 65th anniversaries.In this week's Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Emily Feng brings readers views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro. She was able to see it during a camping trip at altitude.   
   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct
description: Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
body:
Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-155227/nx-s1-mx-6052075-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday, causing the company's stock to soar more than 30%. President Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return. The CEO's comeback follows his resignation just two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including involvement with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, a close ally of the president, had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. His return boosted Nvidia's stock and triggered a rally in the entire stock market, revealing that one man's comeback is worth about a trillion dollars. Some individuals advocating for diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley argue that Huang's return signals that profit is the only priority.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jensen Huang is back atop NVIDIA after the board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director.  "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement.
                
                    Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe
    

   
   🎧 Trump's involvement in a private business decision is significant, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First — even if it's typical for this administration to intervene in the economy. In a CNBC interview, the president said he was concerned that Chinese President Xi Jinping might lure Huang to China to enhance their chip business. Despite mixed economic indicators, Trump frequently highlights stock market performance, noting that Huang reinstatement not only boosted Nvidia's stock but could also uplift the entire market after a tough week.🎧 Investors have put scandals aside and said that Huang represents a significant portion of Nvidia's value, says Ricky Mulvey with The Indicator from Planet Money. The stock trades at about 10 times forward earnings, indicating investors expect to pay for 10 years of future profits now. Investors are paying more for other chipmakers, implying they have more expected future growth, Mulvey says. Despite Nvidia's recent sales doubling over the past year, its investors aren't anticipating much growth ahead.   
   Ukraine recently sank a Russian warship in Libya, while Russian missiles struck Poland. There has been no comment from the Kremlin on the strikes. Depending on perspective, Russia's war in Ukraine appears to be either escalating or de-escalating. This month, the Trump administration said it is making progress towards a negotiated peace. However, fighting has expanded into Eastern and Northern Europe and the Mediterranean.   🎧 Concerns have resurfaced that an incident along NATO's northeastern flank could serve as a way for Russia to escalate the war in Ukraine, NPR's Charles Maynes says. Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Russia is seeking direct confrontation with NATO. Recent bomb threats, cyber attacks and sabotage have raised suspicions among some in Europe that Russia's security services may be involved, Maynes says. He adds that it appears to be Russia's goal to undermine NATO's core principle of collective security, where an attack on one member is an attack on all.   Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., has announced his resignation from Congress following a bipartisan investigation that found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer. The House Ethics Committee determined that Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances" and disregarding the power imbalance in his relationship with staff. The report says his actions could amount to criminal sexual assault. Gomez, who has represented parts of Los Angeles since 2017, lost his reelection bid this fall to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez says he has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.   
   Today's listen   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Maryana Cavalcanti do Nascimento de Oliveira plays timpani (kettledrums) at the Baccarelli Institute in Heliopolis amidst the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on July 8, 2020 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.
                
                    Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images
    

   
   Move over, violins and pianos. The Seattle Symphony is giving the timpani its moment in the spotlight with a world premiere concerto. Principal timpanist Eric Schweikert, who says he is drawn to the back-of-the-classroom vibe in the orchestra, is stepping up to showcase the versatility of the percussion instrument. The piece offers listeners a look at the timpani's range, including rumbling rolls produced with clever mallet work to imitate the effect of a long note. While Schweikert promises to deliver plenty of the wild, Muppets-style Animal energy audiences crave, he's also ready to keep his fellow musicians on their toes — and show the crowd that kettle drums can sing, too.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Holiday travel can be stressful. Make a plan for potential flight disruptions with these tips.
                
                    Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images
    

   
   Traveling by air for the holidays? AAA forecasts that nearly 6 million travelers will be flying this Thanksgiving, making it essential to know how to handle flight cancellations or delays. Travel experts have shared tips with Life Kit to make the rebooking process easier and ensure you won't miss your holiday celebrations.   ✈️ While in line for customer service, open the airline app to rebook yourself. This speeds up the process, which can make a big difference when hundreds of other passengers may be in the same situation.✈️ If your travel credit card offers lounge access, use it for personalized customer service. If you lack access, consider buying an on-site day pass.✈️ Ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they refuse alternative options such as later flights or travel vouchers.✈️ Choose the early-morning flight when rebooking. It's your best chance to avoid delays or cancellations. First flights out have a lower risk of waiting for an incoming aircraft, since the aircraft is likely to have been at the airport overnight.   Are you traveling with a baby or toddler this holiday season? Here is what you should pack. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The new season of Sesame Street focuses on kindness.
                
                    Sesame Workshop
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sesame Workshop
    

   
   Parents of young children say they're worried about a perceived decline in kindness and they now value empathy over manners and compassion over confidence, according to a Sesame Workshop survey.A near-record number of travelers are set to hit the roads this Thanksgiving week. They'll face higher costs due to elevated fuel prices.Has a political or social issue damaged an important relationship for you? If you're thinking about repairing it this holiday season, NPR wants to hear your story.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
